source_text: MULTA et magna sunt, fratres charissimi beneficia divina quibus in salutem nostram Dei Patris et Christi larga et copiosa clementia et operata sit et semper operetur, quod conservandis ac vivificandis nobis Pater Filium misit, ut reparare nos posset, quodque Filius missus esse et hominis filius fieri voluit ut nos Dei filios faceret. Humiliavit se, ut populum qui prius jacebat erigeret: vulneratus est, ut vulnera nostra curaret: servivit, ut ad libertatem servientes extraheret: mori sustinuit, ut immortalitatem mortalibus exhiberet. Multa haec sunt et magna divinae misericordiae munera. Sed adhuc, qualis providentia illa et quanta clementia est quod nobis salutari ratione prospicitur, ut homini qui redemptus est reservando plenius consulatur! Nam, cum Dominus adveniens sanasset illa quae Adam portaverat vulnera, et venena serpentis antiqua curasset, legem dedit sano, et praecepit ne ultra jam peccaret, ne quid peccanti gravius eveniret. Coarctati eramus et in angustum innocentiae praescriptione conclusi. Nec haberet quid fragilitatis humanae infirmitas atque imbecillitas faceret, nisi iterum pietas divina subveniens, justitiae et misericordiae operibus ostensis, viam quamdam tuendae salutis aperiret, ut sordes postmodum, quascumque contrahimus, eleemosynis abluamus. Loquitur in Scripturis divinis Spiritus sanctus et dicit: Eleemosynis et fide delicta purgantur. Non utique illa delicta quae fuerant ante contracta, nam illa Christi sanguine et sanctificatione purgantur. Item denuo dicit: Sicut aqua extinguit ignem, sic eleemosyna extinguit peccatum. Hic quoque ostenditur et probatur quia, sicut lavacro aquae salutaris gehennae ignis extinguitur, ita et eleemosynis atque operationibus justis delictorum flamma sopitur. Et quia semel in Baptismo remissa peccatorum datur, assidua et jugis operatio Baptismi instar imitata, Dei rursus indulgentiam largitur. Hoc et in Evangelio Dominus docet. Nam cum denotarentur discipuli ejus quod ederent, nec prius manus abluissent, respondit et dixit: Qui fecit quod intus est, fecit et quod foris est. Verum date eleemosynam, et ecce vobis munda omnia: docens scilicet et ostendens non manus lavandas esse, sed pectus, et sordes intrinsecus potius quam extrinsecus detrahendas; verum qui purgaverit quod est intus, eum quoque id quod foris est repurgasse, et emundata mente, cute quoque et corpore mundum esse coepisse. Porro autem, monens et ostendens unde mundi et purgati esse possimus, addidit eleemosynas esse faciendas. Misericors docet et monet misericordiam fieri; et quia servare quaerit quos magno pretio redemit, post Baptismi gratiam sordidatos docet denuo posse purgari. Agnoscamus itaque, fratres charissimi, divinae indulgentiae munus salubre, et emundandis purgandisque peccatis nostris, qui sine aliquo conscientiae vulnere esse non possumus, medelis spiritalibus vulnera nostra curemus. Nec quisquam sic sibi de puro atque immaculato pectore blandiatur, ut, innocentia sua fretus, medicinam non putet adhibendam esse vulneribus, cum scriptum sit: Quis gloriabitur castum se habere cor, aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a peccatis? et iterum in Epistola sua Joannes ponat et dicat: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est. Si autem nemo esse sine peccato potest, et quisquis inculpatum se esse dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est, quam necessaria, quam benigna est divina clementia, quae, cum sciat non deesse sanatis quaedam postmodum vulnera, dedit curandis denuo sanandisque vulneribus remedia salutaria! Numquam denique, fratres dilectissimi, admonitio divina cessavit et tacuit quominus in Scripturis sanctis tam veteribus quam novis semper et ubique ad misericordiae opera Dei populus provocaretur; et canente atque exhortante Spiritu sancto, quisquis ad spem regni coelestis instruitur, facere eleemosynas jubetur. Mandat et praecipit Esaiae Deus: Exclama, inquit, in fortitudine, et noli parcere. Sicut tuba exalta vocem tuam, et annuntia plebi meae peccata ipsorum et domui Jacob facinora eorum. Et cum peccata eis sua exprobrari praecepisset, cumque eorum facinora pleno indignationis impetu protulisset, dixissetque eos nec, si orationibus et precibus et jejuniis uterentur, satisfacere pro delictis posse, nec, si in cilicio et cinere volverentur, iram Dei posse lenire, in novissima tamen parte, demonstrans solis eleemosynis Deum posse placari, addidit dicens: Frange esurienti panem tuum, et egenos sine tecto induc in domum tuam. Si videris nudum, vesti eum, et domesticos seminis tui non despicias. Tunc erumpet temporaneum lumen tuum, et vestimenta tua cito orientur, et praeibit ante te justitia, et claritas Dei circumdabit te. Tunc exclamabis, et Deus exaudiet te. Dum adhuc loqueris dicet: Ecce adsum.
pass_a_gloss: Many and great are the divine benefits by which God the Father and Christ have worked and are working for our salvation, because the Father sent the Son to preserve and give life to us, so that He might restore us, and because the Son willed to be sent and to become the son of man, so that He might make us sons of God. He humbled Himself, so that He might raise up the people who were previously lying down: He was wounded, so that He might heal our wounds: He served, so that He might lead servants to freedom: He endured death, so that He might show immortality to mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy. But, moreover, what kind of providence and how great is the mercy by which we are looked after for our salvation, so that the person who has been redeemed might be more fully advised? For, when the Lord came and healed the wounds that Adam had borne, and cured the ancient poisons of the serpent, He gave a law to the healthy, and commanded that they not sin again, lest something worse happen to the sinner. We were restricted and enclosed in a narrow prescription of innocence. And human fragility and weakness would have nothing to do, unless divine piety, helping again, might show works of justice and mercy, and open a certain way of preserving salvation, so that we might wash away the filth that we contract afterwards with alms. The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: Sins are purified by alms and faith. Not, indeed, those sins that were previously contracted, for those are purified by the blood of Christ and sanctification. Again, He says: Just as water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguish sin. Here, also, it is shown and proven that, just as the fire of Gehenna is extinguished by the bath of saving water, so also the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. And because, once in Baptism, the remission of sins is given, a constant and daily operation, imitating Baptism, again obtains God's indulgence. The Lord teaches this also in the Gospel. For when His disciples were rebuked because they were eating without first washing their hands, He responded and said: He who made what is inside, also made what is outside. But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you: teaching, namely, and showing that not the hands, but the heart, are to be washed, and that the filth inside is to be drawn out rather than what is outside; and that he who purifies what is inside, has also purified what is outside, and, with a cleansed mind, has begun to be clean in body and skin. Moreover, warning and showing from where we can be clean and purified, He added that alms are to be given. The Merciful One teaches and warns to have mercy; and because He seeks to keep those whom He redeemed at a great price, after the grace of Baptism, He teaches that those who have been stained can again be purified. Let us recognize, therefore, brothers, the healthy gift of divine indulgence, and, to cleanse and purify our sins, which we cannot be without any wound of conscience, let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies. And let no one flatter himself about having a pure and immaculate heart, so that, trusting in his own innocence, he might not think that medicine is to be applied to wounds, since it is written: Who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sins? And again, John says in his Epistle: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if no one can be without sin, and whoever says that he is blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary, how kind is divine mercy, which, knowing that the healthy do not lack some wounds afterwards, gave remedies for healing and saving wounds again! Never, finally, brothers, has divine admonition ceased and been silent, so that the people of God might not be provoked to works of mercy in the holy Scriptures, both old and new, always and everywhere; and with the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms. God commands and orders Isaiah: Cry out, He says, with strength, and do not spare. Just as a trumpet raises its voice, announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their wicked deeds. And when He had commanded that their sins be rebuked, and their wicked deeds be brought forth with a full impulse of indignation, and had said that they could not satisfy for their sins, even if they used prayers and supplications and fasts, nor could they placate the wrath of God, even if they rolled in sackcloth and ashes, in the last part, however, showing that God can be placated only by alms, He added, saying: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise the poor of your family. Then your light will break forth, and your garments will quickly shine, and justice will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking, He will say: Behold, I am here.

bible_refs.note: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless into your house

pass_b_english: Many and great are the divine benefits by which God the Father and Christ have worked, and continue to work, for our salvation. The Father sent the Son to preserve us and give us life so that He might restore us, and the Son willingly allowed Himself to be sent and to become human so that He might make us children of God. He humbled Himself in order to raise up a people who had previously lain prostrate. He was wounded so that He might heal our wounds. He served so that He might lead servants into freedom. He endured death so that He might offer immortality to mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy.

But beyond this, consider what kind of providence and how great the mercy is by which we are watched over for our salvation, so that the person who has been redeemed might be more fully provided for. When the Lord came, He healed the wounds that Adam had borne and cured the ancient poisons of the serpent. He gave a law to the healthy and commanded them not to sin again, lest something worse befall the sinner. We were restricted and confined within a narrow prescription of innocence. Human frailty and weakness would have had no recourse unless divine piety came to our aid once more. By showing works of justice and mercy, it opened a way to preserve our salvation, so that we might wash away whatever filth we contract afterward through alms.

The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: 'Sins are purified by alms and faith' (Proverbs 16:6). This does not refer, of course, to sins contracted beforehand; those are purified by the blood of Christ and by sanctification. Again He says: 'Just as water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguishes sin' (Sirach 3:30). Here it is also shown and proven that, just as the fire of Gehenna is extinguished by the bath of saving water, so also the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. Because the remission of sins is given once in Baptism, a constant and daily practice that imitates Baptism again obtains God's indulgence.

The Lord teaches this also in the Gospel. When His disciples were rebuked for eating without first washing their hands, He responded: 'He who made what is inside also made what is outside. But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you' (Luke 11:40-41). He was teaching and showing that it is not the hands but the heart that must be washed, and that the filth inside must be drawn out rather than what is outside. He showed that whoever purifies what is inside has also purified what is outside, and that with a cleansed mind, the skin and body also begin to be clean. Moreover, warning and showing from where we can be clean and purified, He added that alms are to be given. The Merciful One teaches and urges us to show mercy. Because He seeks to keep those whom He redeemed at a great price, He teaches that those stained after the grace of Baptism can be purified again.

Let us therefore recognize, brothers, the salutary gift of divine indulgence. Since we cannot be without some wound of conscience, let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies to cleanse and purify our sins. Let no one flatter himself about having a pure and immaculate heart, so that, trusting in his own innocence, he thinks medicine need not be applied to wounds. It is written: 'Who will boast that he has a chaste heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin?' (Proverbs 20:9). And again John says in his Epistle: 'If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us' (1 John 1:8). If no one can be without sin, and whoever claims to be blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary and how kind is divine mercy! Knowing that the healthy do not lack certain wounds afterward, God gave remedies to heal and save those wounds again.

Finally, brothers, divine admonition has never ceased or been silent, so that in the holy Scriptures, both old and new, always and everywhere, God's people are urged to works of mercy. With the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms. God commands and orders Isaiah: 'Cry out with strength, do not hold back. Raise your voice like a trumpet. Announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their wicked deeds' (Isaiah 58:1). After commanding that their sins be rebuked and their wicked deeds be brought forth with a full impulse of indignation, He declared that they could not satisfy for their sins even with prayers, supplications, and fasts, nor could they placate God's wrath even by rolling in sackcloth and ashes. Yet in the last part, showing that God can be placated only by alms, He added: 'Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own flesh and blood' (Isaiah 58:7). 'Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will quickly appear. Your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will be your rear guard. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry for help, and He will say: Here I am' (Isaiah 58:8-9).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering with necessary scripture citations (Proverbs 16:6, Sirach 3:30, Luke 11:40-41, Proverbs 20:9, 1 John 1:8, Isaiah 58:1, 58:7, 58:8-9) which correspond to the quoted/alluded passages in the Latin. The title 'Divine Mercy and Alms' correctly names the thought. All clauses, including the complex descriptions of Christ's work and the Isaiah passage, are preserved.
